abstracts.abstract: The prediction of protein function from sequence data remains a central challenge in computational biology,制约着功能基因组学的发展。传统 methods rely on sequence similarity or homology transfer, which limitations become apparent when analyzing evolutionarily distant proteins or those with novel domain architectures. This study introduces GraphFunc, a paradigm-shifting framework that conceptualizes protein sequences as compositional graphs and leverages heterogeneous graph neural networks for function prediction. The proposed architecture employs a novel attention mechanism that learns contextualized amino acid representations while modeling residue-level interactions through learnable k-mer embeddings. Unlike existing approaches that treat sequences as linear strings, GraphFunc captures higher-order structural relationships inherent in protein sequences, enabling the model to discern subtle sequence-function associations. Comprehensive evaluation across 12 benchmark datasets spanning enzyme commission classification, gene ontology prediction, and pathway annotation demonstrates that GraphFunc achieves an average F1 score improvement of 18.3% over state-of-the-art methods. Remarkably, the framework exhibits superior generalization capability on proteins with less than 30% sequence identity to training examples, suggesting effective learning of sequence-function mappings beyond homology. This work establishes a new theoretical paradigm for protein function prediction and provides insights into how graph-based representations can advance bioinformatics and systems biology research. The GraphFunc framework is freely available at https://github.com/example/GraphFunc.

Accurate prediction of protein secondary structure constitutes a foundational task in structural bioinformatics with implications for protein engineering and drug discovery. Current deep learning approaches achieve approximately 86% accuracy in three-state (helix, strand, coil) prediction, yet performance degrades significantly for proteins lacking known homologs. We present an enhanced transformer architecture, termed StructFormer++, which substantially advances the state-of-the-art through three key innovations: (1) a bidirectional evolutionary encoding mechanism that incorporates multiple sequence alignment information through self-supervised pre-training on 250 million protein sequences, (2) a hierarchical attention mechanism capturing both local and global sequence context, and (3) an uncertainty-aware training objective that explicitly models prediction confidence. Evaluation on the CB513, CullPDB, and CASP13 datasets reveals that StructFormer++ achieves 91.2% Q3 accuracy, representing a 5.4 percentage point improvement over the previous best method. Particularly noteworthy is the model's robustness on proteins with less than 20% sequence identity to training data, where performance improvement reaches 8.1 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component contributes independently to overall performance gains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the uncertainty estimates correlate strongly with prediction accuracy, enabling reliable identification of potentially erroneous predictions. This work advances computational biology by providing both a superior prediction method and interpretable uncertainty quantification for protein secondary structure prediction.

The integration of multi-omics data presents a fundamental challenge in systems biology, as current tools inadequately capture the complex, bidirectional regulatory relationships across genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic layers. We present OmicsFlow, a comprehensive bioinformatics platform that introduces a paradigm shift in multi-omics integration through dynamic Bayesian network modeling and causal inference. The system encompasses four core modules: (1) an automated data preprocessing pipeline supporting 15+ omics data types with standardized quality control, (2) MetaGraph, a novel graph-based integration engine that models cross-omics relationships as dynamic networks, (3) CausalPath, implementing constraint-based causal discovery algorithms to infer directed regulatory relationships, and (4) VizOmics, an interactive visualization suite for exploring integrated networks at multiple biological scales. OmicsFlow uniquely addresses the temporal dimension of biological regulation by incorporating time-series analysis capabilities, enabling the construction of dynamic regulatory models. The platform processes a typical 100-sample multi-omics dataset in approximately 45 minutes on standard computational infrastructure. Validation using synthetic benchmark datasets with known ground truth demonstrates 87% accuracy in recovering causal regulatory relationships. Application to a breast cancer cohort reveals novel regulatory mechanisms involving non-coding RNAs that would be missed by single-omics analysis. OmicsFlow represents a complete re-imagining of multi-omics analysis workflows and is available as a containerized application with comprehensive documentation at https://omicsflow.bio.

RNA sequencing has become indispensable for transcriptomics research, yet current pipelines for differential expression analysis exhibit substantial method-dependent variability, complicating biological interpretation. We introduce RNAFlow 2.0, a substantially enhanced bioinformatics pipeline that addresses critical limitations of existing tools through innovations in statistical modeling and biological annotation. The system advances previous approaches through three major improvements: First, we implement an improved ensemble differential expression method combining edgeR, DESeq2, and a novel shrinkage estimator that reduces false positives by 34% while maintaining statistical power. Second, RNAFlow 2.0 incorporates a deep learning-based batch effect correction module that outperforms existing methods on complex experimental designs with multiple confounding factors. Third, we integrate a comprehensive functional enrichment analysis engine with expanded ontology coverage and pathway databases, including species-specific annotations for 45 organisms. The pipeline processes a typical 24-sample experiment in 25 minutes, representing a 40% speed improvement over RNAFlow 1.0. Validation using synthetic datasets with known true positives demonstrates that RNAFlow 2.0 achieves 92% precision at 85% recall, significantly outperforming individual tools and the previous pipeline version. Case studies on COVID-19 patient transcriptomic data and cancer immunotherapy response datasets illustrate the platform's utility in translational bioinformatics. RNAFlow 2.0 is available as a Docker image with an intuitive web interface at https://rnaflow.bio.
